title: Why MCP Exists: End the N×M Madness
objective: After this lesson you will be able to explain MCP's economic argument (N+M vs N×M integrations), distinguish it from provider function calling, and decide what belongs in MCP servers versus application code.
why: Every assistant team rebuilds the same integrations: catalog lookup for Claude, catalog lookup for the custom app, order tools per provider SDK — bespoke wirings multiplying with hosts × sources. MCP standardizes the seam once: servers expose context and actions, any host consumes them. Adopting it (or not) is an architecture decision with 10x cost implications — this lesson makes it on purpose.

blocks.text: Twelve hosts × eight data sources with bespoke integrations = 96 wirings to build, version, and maintain — each with its own auth, schemas, and failure modes. MCP collapses it to 12 + 8 = 20 protocol implementations: each host speaks MCP once, each server speaks it once, and any pair interoperates. Standards convert quadratic integration cost into linear — the entire economic case in one arithmetic.

blocks.caption: Quadratic vs linear integration cost — the adoption argument

blocks.text: **Function calling** standardizes model→tool *syntax per provider* (OpenAI's format differs from Anthropic's). **MCP** standardizes the *whole integration surface* across hosts and servers: discovery (server/discover), tools (list/call), resources (list/read), prompts, transports, versions. One function-calling integration serves one provider's models; one MCP server serves every host — Claude Code, VS Code, Cursor, custom apps. Different layers, complementary, not competing.

Servers expose **capabilities with stable contracts**: catalog search, order lookup, policy text, triage prompts — versioned, permissioned, auditable. Application logic (routing, orchestration, UI) stays in hosts. The boundary test: would a *second, different host* use this? Catalog lookup yes (server); this quarter's dashboard layout no (app code). Servers are products with consumers plural.

blocks.title: Price your integrations
blocks.note: Run it: 6 vs 5 today (standards barely win small), 96 vs 20 at scale (standards dominate). Adoption math favors growth trajectories — count your roadmap, not just today.

items: N+M vs N×M: standards linearize integration cost — counts compound per added party
Function calling = per-provider syntax; MCP = cross-host standard (discovery, tools, resources, prompts)
Servers hold reusable contracted capabilities; app-specific logic stays in hosts

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice pricer for your org's real host/source counts (stated). (b) Classify three integrations (order lookup, dashboard layout, policy text) as server vs app with the second-host test. (c) State the one condition under which bespoke still wins, honestly.
hints: Plug real numbers: marginal cost per added party is the decision metric, not today's totals.
Order lookup + policy text: servers (reused across hosts). Dashboard layout: app (single-consumer presentation).
Bespoke wins: single host + single source + stable forever (no growth, no reuse) — standards tax simplicity when N=M=1 permanently.
exercise.why: Adoption decisions need org-specific math plus the honest exception: standards serve growth and reuse; permanent singletons don't need them. Say the exception aloud or teams standardize cargo-cult.
exercise.code: // Integration-pricing pattern: totals + marginals + the N=M=1 exception.

quiz.q: Twelve hosts, eight sources, all bespoke. MCP's math?
options: 96 bespoke wirings → 20 protocol implementations (N+M); each added party costs +1, not +N/+M
quiz.explain: Quadratic-to-linear collapse plus compounding marginals: the economic case is arithmetic, not aesthetics.

options: Different layers: per-provider syntax vs cross-host standard (discovery/tools/resources/prompts); complementary
quiz.explain: Syntax standard versus integration standard. One function-calling integration serves one provider; one MCP server serves every host.

quiz.q: Dashboard layout as an MCP server. Verdict?
options: No: single-consumer presentation fails the second-host test — app code, not server capability
quiz.explain: Servers hold reusable contracted capabilities across hosts. Single-use presentation is app code wearing a protocol costume.

summary: N+M economics, complementary layers (not rivals), second-host test for serverhood. Adopt on math; exempt honest singletons.
next: Economics settled — now the machinery: hosts, clients, servers, transports, and the JSON-RPC discovery dance. Next: architecture.
